extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (primary) and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent claim definiteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph), relationship to 35 U.S.C. 101/102/103 and 112(a), and identification/applicability of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means/step-plus-function) limitations. Includes form-paragraph templates and instructions on applying prior art rejections when claim terms are indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use claims lacking active steps may be indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that merely recites a 'use' without setting forth any active, positive steps involved in the process generally raises an issue of indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claim to 'a process for using monoclonal antibodies ... to isolate and purify human fibroblast interferon' held indefinite (Ex parte Erlich). Such 'use' claims that do not purport to claim a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter may also fail 35 U.S.C. 101 (In re Moreton). Consider rejection under 112(b) and/or 101 where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims cannot import specification limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a claim should be interpreted in light of the specification disclosure, it is generally improper to read limitations contained in the specification into the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on the specification to impart limitations to the claim that are not recited in the claim. See In re Prater and In re Winkhaus for discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use claims may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 and/or 112
rubrics_metrics.description: It is appropriate to reject a claim that recites a use but fails to recite steps under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112(b) if the facts support both rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When facts support both grounds, make both rejections so applicant can address them; cite appropriate form paragraphs for 112(b) (see MPEP §2175).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Utilizing' or similar step can be definite in some cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of a step such as 'utilizing' has been held not indefinite where the step is clear in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ex parte Porter — a claim reciting the step of 'utilizing the nozzle of claim 7' was found not indefinite. Evaluate context and whether the step imparts sufficient meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omnibus claims are indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: An omnibus claim (e.g., 'A device substantially as shown and described') should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as indefinite for failing to point out what is included or excluded by the claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Ex parte Fressola for history/explanation. Use form paragraph 7.35 to reject omnibus claims; see MPEP §1302.04(b) for cancellation upon allowance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference to figures/tables only when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporation by reference to a specific figure or table in a claim is permitted only in exceptional circumstances where there is no practical way to define the invention in words and where incorporation is more concise than duplicating a drawing or table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporation by reference is a 'necessity doctrine', not for applicant convenience (Ex parte Fressola). Where possible, claims should be complete in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference characters in claims generally don't affect scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference characters corresponding to elements recited in the detailed description and the drawings may be used in conjunction with recitation of the same element or group of elements in the claims; generally their presence or absence does not affect claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §608.01(m) for treatment of reference characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical formula/compound claims not indefinite absent error
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to chemical compounds and compositions are not to be considered indefinite or speculative merely because a structure is not fully presented or because corroborating spectroscopic/other data are absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/cases: Ex parte Morton; Ex parte Sobin; In re Fisher reversed a rejection for failure to identify entire structure. Compounds may be claimed by a name understandable to one skilled in the art, by physical/chemical characteristics, or by the process by which they are made (Ex parte Brian). The absence of corroborating data alone is not a basis for indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademarks/trade names in claims require careful analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of a trademark or trade name in a claim is not per se improper under 35 U.S.C. 112(b), but the claim must be analyzed to determine how the mark or name is used in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A trademark identifies source, not the goods; if used to identify/describe a particular material or product, the claim fails 112(b) (Ex parte Simpson). If present but not intended as a limitation, explain why; if it causes confusion as to scope, reject under 112(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims shouldn't be rejected solely for defining inherent function of an apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Method/process claims should not be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) merely because they define the inherent function of a disclosed machine or apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Tarczy-Hornoch: an otherwise patentable process claim should not be rejected simply because the application discloses an apparatus that will inherently carry out the recited steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution: identify all grounds and explain indefinite term interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should review each claim for compliance with every statutory requirement in the initial review and identify all applicable grounds of rejection in the first Office action; when a claim term renders a claim indefinite, the examiner should make an indefiniteness rejection and also any prior-art rejections based on the examiner's interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite 37 CFR 1.104(a)(1) and MPEP §706. Avoid piecemeal examination; reject each claim on all valid grounds available (see MPEP §707.07(g)). When rejecting over prior art in view of an indefiniteness issue, explicitly state how the claim term is being interpreted relative to the applied prior art (see In re Packard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approaches for prior art rejection when claim terms are indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Two approaches: (1) If uncertainty is not great and at least one interpretation renders claim unpatentable, enter two rejections — indefiniteness under 112(b) and prior art under the interpretation that makes the prior art applicable; (2) If there is great confusion/uncertainty as to interpretation, do not base a 103 rejection on speculation about meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach (1) helps avoid piecemeal examination and gives applicant clearer notice (see Ex parte Ionescu). Approach (2) is supported by In re Steele — do not base a 103 rejection on considerable speculation about claim meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and 112(b) are distinct requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description/enabling disclosure) and 112(b) (particularity/distinctness) are separate and distinct; insufficient disclosure under 112(a) does not by itself render the claim indefinite under 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification discloses that a particular feature is essential to practice of the invention, failure to recite that feature in the claim may support a rejection under 112(a) (In re Mayhew). If a claim is amended to include subject matter not described in the application as filed, reject under 112(a) (In re Simon, In re Panagrossi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use form paragraphs for 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific form paragraphs (7.30.02, 7.34–7.34.15, 7.35, 7.35.01, etc.) should be used to make rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ¶7.30.02 quotes the statute and notes when to use it (first actions on merits and final rejections). Paragraphs 7.34.x provide templates for common indefiniteness issues; ensure proper sequencing (e.g., 7.30.02 precedes 7.34.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.34.01 Failure to Particularly Point Out and Distinctly Claim (Indefinite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph to reject claims as indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter the inventor regards as the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. Follow with one or more of form paragraphs 7.34.02–7.34.10 and/or 7.34.23–7.34.24 as applicable. Identify particular term(s)/limitation(s) rendering claim indefinite and explain why; if scope is ascertainable to one of ordinary skill, do not use this rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.34.02 Terminology Used Inconsistent with Accepted Meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use when applicant's use/definition of a term is inconsistent with accepted meaning and the specification does not clearly redefine it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applicant acts as own lexicographer, the written description must clearly redefine the term. Provide citation/support for accepted meaning when asserting inconsistency (textbook/dictionary). Precede with 7.30.02 and 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.34.03 Relative Term/Term of Degree Rendering Claim Indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: A relative term or term of degree (e.g., 'sufficient', 'substantial') that is not defined and provides no standard for ascertaining the requisite degree renders the claim indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain which parameter or limitation is rendered indefinite. Precede with 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.34.04 Broad Range and Narrow Range in Same Claim May Be Indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting both a broad range/limitation together with a narrower range/limitation that falls within it may be indefinite if the claim does not clearly set forth the metes and bounds of the protection desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain whether the narrower language is merely exemplary or required; see MPEP §2173.05(c). Precede with 7.34.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.34.10 Indefinite Claim Language: 'Such As'
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'such as' renders a claim indefinite because it is unclear whether limitations following the phrase are part of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form paragraph must be preceded by 7.34.01; may be modified to fit other instances of indefiniteness. See MPEP §2173.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.34.08 Indefinite Claim Language: 'For Example'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the phrase 'for example' renders the claim indefinite because it is unclear whether the limitations following are part of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by 7.34.01. See MPEP §2173.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.34.09 Indefinite Claim Language: 'Or The Like'
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'or the like' renders claim(s) indefinite because it includes elements not actually disclosed, making scope unascertainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by 7.34.01. See MPEP §2173.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.34.05 Lack of Antecedent Basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use when a claim recites a limitation without sufficient antecedent basis in the claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by 7.34.01. In bracket identify the limitation lacking antecedent basis (e.g., 'said lever') and where it appears in the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.34.12 Essential Steps Omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected for being incomplete due to omission of essential steps, amounting to a gap between steps (process claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only in aggravated situations where omission makes scope indeterminate. Precede with 7.30.02 or 7.103 and 7.34.01. Recite omitted steps and rationale for considering them critical/essential (see MPEP §2172.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.34.07/7.34.13 Claims as Literal Translations/Essential Elements Omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are narrative and indefinite, appearing to be literal translations with grammatical/idiomatic errors, or claims omitting essential elements, should be rejected as indefinite/incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with 7.34.01. For omitted elements, recite omitted elements and explain why they are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.34.14 Essential Cooperative Relationships Omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject claims that omit essential structural cooperative relationships of elements, creating a gap between necessary structural connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precede with 7.30.02 or 7.103 and 7.34.01. Recite omitted cooperative relationships and rationale for their essentiality (see MPEP §2172.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.34.15 Rejection Under 35 U.S.C. 112 for Pro Se Applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance for rejecting claims filed by pro se applicants that are narrative in form and replete with indefinite language; the structure must be clearly and positively specified and claims must be in one-sentence form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when applicant acts pro se; note claim format expectations and reference patents cited to illustrate claim format.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.35 Rejection for Omnibus Claim (Form Paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph to reject an omnibus type claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as indefinite for failing to point out what is included or excluded by the claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by 7.30.02 or 7.103. No further explanation necessary for omnibus-type claims. Example: 'A device substantially as shown and described.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.35.01 Trademark/Trade Name as a Limitation (Form Paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim containing a trademark/trade name used as a limitation to identify or describe a particular material or product does not comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert trademark/trade name and where used in claim; specify the material/product claimed to be identified/ described by the mark; explain why identification/description is indefinite (see Ex parte Simpson). Precede with 7.30.02 or 7.103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) general guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Section provides guidelines for examination of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 112 sixth-paragraph 'means or step plus function' limitations; BRI for such language is the structure, material or act described in the specification as performing the entire claimed function and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts (In re Donaldson, Williamson) require that examiners consider the specification's corresponding structure and apply the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the written description. 112(f) limitations may receive a narrower interpretation than non-112(f) limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that 112(f) applies when 'means' or 'step' used
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation is presumed to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) when it explicitly uses the term 'means' or 'step' and includes functional language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption is overcome if the limitation includes sufficient structure, material, or acts necessary to perform the recited function (TriMed, Altiris). If examiner decides 'means'/'step' limitation is not treated under 112(f), state reasons in Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that 112(f) does NOT apply when 'means' not used (rebuttable)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation that does not use the term 'means' will trigger the rebuttable presumption that 35 U.S.C. 112(f) does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption is overcome when the claim term fails to recite sufficiently definite structure or recites function without reciting sufficient structure (Williamson; Watts). Examiner should still consider whether the presumption is overcome and may apply 112(f) where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-prong analysis for applying 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners will apply 35 U.S.C. 112(f) to a claim limitation if it meets a 3-prong analysis: (A) uses 'means'/'step' or generic placeholder; (B) is modified by functional language (e.g., 'means for', 'configured to'); (C) is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all three prongs met, treat as 112(f). If claim uses 'means'/'step' but prong (B) or (C) not met, the Office action must explain why 112(f) is not being applied. Explicitly state in Office action when a claim limitation is being interpreted under 112(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI rule for 112(f) limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim limitation invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f) is the structure, material, or act described in the specification as performing the claimed function and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not disregard the structure disclosed in the specification when rendering a patentability determination (In re Donaldson). 112(f) can lead to a narrower claim construction than non-112(f) claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-language-driven application of 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) is driven by the claim language, not by applicant intent or statements in the specification or prosecution history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must construe claim terms as they would be by one of ordinary skill in the art in light of the specification. Applicants have the opportunity and obligation to define their inventions precisely during prosecution (In re Morris, In re Zletz, Sage Prods.).
